headline: A rough day across the board — PLS.AX hammered 4.5%, MSFT and TTWO both slid hard last night, while gold hits record highs and the RBA signals more pain ahead.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: Pilbara had a tough session today, dropping 4.5% to $6.14. Despite some positive noise from Citi upgrading lithium price targets for major Chinese lithium producers, the broader lithium sector remains under pressure — weak global demand signals and India's industrial slowdown are weighing on the commodity outlook. PLS is now down 8.9% overall on your cost base.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft dropped 3.2% last night to $427.34, and is now slightly underwater (-3.6%) on your investment. No single major catalyst — but investor sentiment has shifted a bit as the market reassesses AI spending growth timelines. Despite that, Microsoft's AI chief Mustafa Suleyman publicly flagged Anthropic (not Google or Meta) as the company's biggest worry, suggesting the competitive landscape is tightening.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two fell nearly 3% last night to $215.80, extending losses on your position to -6.9%. The main noise around TTWO right now is GTA 6 buzz getting chaotic — police were called after fans literally broke into the Rockstar Games office, which isn't exactly reassuring for the brand. No earnings or guidance updates; this looks like general market softness dragging on growth/gaming stocks.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI dropped 2.4% today to $18.37, now sitting -3.5% below your cost base. The AI ETF is tracking weakness in big tech names like MSFT and GOOG, which make up a large chunk of its holdings. No specific GXAI catalyst — it's riding the broader tech selloff.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: Google dipped a modest 0.76% last night to $355.68, though you're still up a healthy 23% overall on this position. The slight softness follows some analyst commentary questioning whether Google is losing ground to OpenAI and Anthropic in the AI race — but Alphabet did hold its investor presentation this week, and revenue growth prospects remain solid. Small move; nothing to panic about.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG dipped 1% today to $75.86, following the broader ASX 200 which fell 1.1%. As a diversified growth fund with heavy global equities exposure, VDHG naturally tracks both ASX and US market weakness — today's pullback reflects that general risk-off tone across markets. Still slightly in the green overall (+0.64%).

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE eased 0.64% today to $92.90, a relatively mild dip compared to the broader market. Emerging markets have been dragged by a softer AUD/USD (the Aussie dollar fell 0.6% today) and general global risk aversion. Your position is essentially flat overall, down just $0.38.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS had the smallest dip of the day, slipping 0.45% to $520.21. The ASX-listed US market ETF mirrors the US total market, and last night's S&P 500 and NASDAQ weakness is feeding through to today's price. Still up 0.87% on your overall position.

movers.name: BetaShares Global Energy Companies ETF
movers.note: FUEL was the one bright spot today, nudging up 0.8% to $8.77 — the only holding in the green. Global energy stocks are holding up as oil prices remain elevated around US$95/barrel. There's also a ratings upgrade for Exxon Mobil (a major FUEL holding) as shares track the oil rebound. FUEL is now up 3.69% on your cost base.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Hold, but watch closely
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals fell 4.5% today to $6.14, the single worst mover in your portfolio. Your position is down 8.9% overall. Citi has turned bullish on lithium prices and lifted targets for major Chinese lithium producers, which is a green shoot — but the near-term price action is ugly. No need to panic sell, but worth watching whether this stabilises or keeps bleeding.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Hold, but last night's 3.2% drop stings
watch_today.detail: Microsoft fell 3.2% last night and is now slightly underwater on your cost base. The AI spending story is under scrutiny as competition from Anthropic heats up. No major earnings or guidance updates, but sentiment has softened. Nothing broken fundamentally — hold and wait for clarity, but keep an eye on this week's US tech tone.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — Hold through AI sector turbulence
watch_today.detail: Your AI ETF dropped 2.4% today, dragged down by weakness in its big tech holdings (MSFT, GOOG). Trump's new AI executive order is creating some regulatory uncertainty for OpenAI, Google and Anthropic — companies that make up a big chunk of GXAI. The long-term AI theme is intact, but expect volatility while the policy picture settles.

watch_today.title: RBA signals more pain — rates not falling fast
watch_today.detail: RBA Governor Bullock warned today that inflation is likely to rise further in the near term, and the Bank is flagging up to two more years of economic pressure. Australia's GDP is growing at 2.5% annually but a slowdown is beginning. This matters for your ASX holdings — higher rates for longer typically weigh on growth assets and property. One bank is predicting conditions not seen in 15 years for millions of Aussies.

watch_today.title: Gold hits $4,490 — a safe-haven surge worth noting
watch_today.detail: Gold jumped 1.2% last night to US$4,490/oz, an eye-catching level. When gold runs this hard while stocks fall, it usually signals investors are nervous about something bigger — whether that's geopolitical risk, inflation, or a slowing economy. You don't hold gold directly, but this backdrop is worth watching: it tends to precede broader market caution.

watch_today.title: FUEL.AX — Hold, energy is the portfolio standout
watch_today.detail: FUEL was your only green holding today, up 0.8% with oil sitting firm near US$95/barrel. Exxon Mobil got a ratings upgrade today, and despite some demand headwinds from India's industrial slowdown, the global energy sector is holding up. No reason to sell — this is doing what you want it to do.

markets.summary: It was a sea of red on Thursday. The ASX 200 closed down 1.13% to 8,686 — a drop of nearly 100 points — as investors reacted to last night's weak Wall Street session and RBA commentary signalling a difficult period ahead. Last night, the S&P 500 fell 0.74% and the NASDAQ dropped 0.89%, with big tech like MSFT and TTWO leading losses. Oil eased slightly to US$95.21 but remains elevated. The standout was gold, which surged 1.2% to US$4,490 — a safe-haven signal that markets are nervous. The Aussie dollar slipped 0.6% to 71.3 US cents, which nudges up the AUD value of your US holdings slightly.

indicators.note: Closed down 1.13% today — broad-based selloff across tech and growth sectors.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Last night's session: fell 0.74%, dragged by tech weakness.

indicators.name: NASDAQ
indicators.note: Last night: down 0.89%, MSFT and growth stocks the main culprits.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Slight easing but still elevated near US$95 — supportive for FUEL.AX.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Surged 1.2% — investors piling into safe havens amid market uncertainty.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: Aussie dollar slipped 0.6% — slightly boosts the AUD value of your US holdings (GOOG, MSFT, TTWO).

politics.summary: The RBA dominated domestic headlines today, with Governor Bullock warning that inflation is likely to get worse before it gets better. Fiscal tensions are also building, with SA taking a dig at Treasurer Chalmers as federal debt heads toward a record $54 billion, and the Greens and Liberals joining forces to delay budget legislation. In media, Meta went on the offensive against the government's proposed journalism levy.

stories.title: RBA warns inflation likely to rise further — two more years of pain ahead
stories.why_it_matters: RBA Governor Michele Bullock said today that inflation is likely to rise further in the near term, and the Bank is signalling up to two more years of economic difficulty. That means interest rates — the cost of your mortgage or personal loans — are staying higher for longer. One major Australian bank is warning of conditions not seen in 15 years for millions of Aussies. For investors, this is a headwind for growth assets and property values.

stories.title: AI boom contributed to the RBA's interest rate U-turn, says AFR
stories.why_it_matters: The AFR reports that the unexpected global AI investment boom was a key factor in the RBA reversing its earlier expectation of rate cuts. Massive spending on AI infrastructure — data centres, chips, energy — has kept global inflation stickier than expected. Basically, the AI buildout has been so large it's actually moved the needle on central bank decisions. Good for AI stocks long-term, but painful for borrowers right now.

stories.title: Federal budget heading for record $54b debt — SA takes a dig at Chalmers
stories.why_it_matters: South Australia has publicly criticised Treasurer Jim Chalmers as the federal government's budget deficit heads toward a record $54 billion in debt. The Greens and Liberals are also working together to delay budget legislation in parliament. This level of fiscal pressure — the government spending far more than it earns — can put upward pressure on inflation and bond yields (which is the rate at which the government borrows money), making the RBA's job even harder.

stories.title: Meta calls Albanese's journalism levy 'indefensible'
stories.why_it_matters: Meta has hit back hard at the Albanese government's proposed journalism levy, calling it 'indefensible'. The levy would force big tech platforms like Facebook and Instagram to pay into a fund supporting Australian news publishers. Meta argues it already supports Australian journalism and shouldn't be taxed further. This is the latest round of the ongoing fight between Canberra and Silicon Valley over who pays for news — a battle that's been heating up since the News Media Bargaining Code passed in 2021.

ai.summary: AI regulation is the big theme today — Trump signed a new executive order that could reshape how OpenAI, Google and Anthropic launch new models in the US. Meanwhile, Microsoft's AI chief called out Anthropic (not Google) as the company's biggest rival, and a tech commentator made a blunt case that Google is genuinely falling behind in the AI race.

stories.title: Trump's new AI executive order could change how OpenAI, Google and Anthropic launch models
stories.why_it_matters: The Trump White House has released a new executive order focused on 'Advanced AI Innovation and Security' — essentially a set of rules that could dictate how and when AI companies can release new models. Unlike the Biden-era approach which leaned toward safety guardrails, Trump's order appears to prioritise speed and US competitiveness over caution. Critics — including Australia's own ASPI think tank — say it won't be enough to match China's AI push, and lacks meaningful oversight. For your GOOG, MSFT, and GXAI.AX holdings, this is worth watching: lighter regulation generally speeds up AI deployment, which is good for revenues.

stories.title: Microsoft AI chief: Anthropic is our biggest worry — not Google, Meta or OpenAI
stories.why_it_matters: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said in a fresh interview that his team is 'more concerned' about Anthropic (the company behind the Claude AI assistant) than about Google, Meta, or even OpenAI. He described Anthropic as the sharpest competitive threat in enterprise AI — that is, AI tools used by businesses. This is a notable shift: it suggests the AI race isn't just a two-horse Google vs Microsoft contest. For MSFT investors, it signals the company knows it needs to keep investing heavily to stay ahead.

stories.title: Is Google falling behind in the AI race? One commentator says the risk is 'company-destroying'
stories.why_it_matters: Prominent tech commentator M.G. Siegler published a sharp piece arguing that Google is genuinely lagging behind OpenAI and Anthropic, that the shift to standalone AI apps (like ChatGPT) rather than search is a huge structural challenge for Alphabet, and that strategic missteps could be 'company-destroying'. This is a minority view — Google remains enormously profitable — but it's a real risk thread worth watching for anyone holding GOOG. Alphabet held its investor presentation this week and is talking up its AI roadmap, but the market pressure is real.

stories.title: AI tools have triggered a coding revolution — but software engineers are figuring out what's next
stories.why_it_matters: Business Insider reports that AI coding tools have so fundamentally changed software development that engineers are now genuinely rethinking their role — less time writing code from scratch, more time reviewing, directing, and problem-solving what AI generates. This is relevant for your holdings: it signals that AI is already having a real-world productivity effect, which supports the long-term bull case for companies like Google and Microsoft that are embedding AI into developer tools.

sport.summary: NRL Round 14 kicks off tonight with Sea Eagles vs Rabbitohs at 4 Pines Park (7:50 PM). The Titans face a tough trip to Suncorp on Saturday — local Gold Coast interest. There's also a big AFL weekend with 10,000 American fans descending on Melbourne, and a Tigers star dropping a bombshell about loyalty ahead of Round 14.

stories.title: NRL Round 14 tips: Expert picks for every game
stories.why_it_matters: Round 14 starts tonight with Sea Eagles hosting the Rabbitohs at 4 Pines Park (7:50 PM). The big local game for Gold Coast fans is Saturday night — Broncos vs Titans at Suncorp Stadium (7:35 PM). The Cowboys host the Dolphins on Saturday arvo too (5:30 PM, Townsville). Warriors have the bye this round.

stories.title: 'I'll never be loyal to a club': Tigers star's shock warning — and why Benji is at the centre
stories.why_it_matters: A Wests Tigers star has made a headline-grabbing declaration that he'll 'never be loyal to a club,' with Fox Sports reporting that coach Benji Marshall is at the centre of the contract uncertainty. The Tigers face the Panthers on Sunday (2:00 PM at CommBank Stadium) in a game that now carries extra off-field intrigue. Loyalty dramas like this can destabilise squads heading into big games.

stories.title: AFL's massive US weekend: 10,000 American fans to paint Melbourne red
stories.why_it_matters: This weekend is shaping up as one of the AFL's biggest international moments — 10,000 American fans are expected to descend on Melbourne for a marquee round. The Age reports the AFL's top 10 ladder is unusually tight this season, making the round a genuine game-changer for finals positioning. It's a big moment for the AFL's push to crack the US market, which has been a long-term strategic goal for the competition.

stories.title: NRL plots huge event for Arrow as he eyes AFL switch
stories.why_it_matters: The NRL is reportedly planning a major event around Arrow — a talented young player who has attracted interest from AFL clubs. News.com.au reports the NRL is trying to keep him in rugby league by making him the centrepiece of a showcase occasion. Cross-code poaching has been a recurring storyline in 2026, and the NRL is clearly taking the threat seriously enough to put on a show.
